title: Rotation and the wind: Coriolis, inertial oscillations, geostrophic balance
desc: On a rotating planet a free particle in the horizontal plane moves in inertial circles of radius v/f with period 2π/f, f = 2Ω sin φ (left panel, in the rotating frame). Right: a steady wind in balance between the pressure-gradient force and the Coriolis force blows along the isobars (geostrophic), with low pressure on its left in the Northern Hemisphere; friction turns it across the isobars toward low pressure.
chapters: CL12 Rotating Frames and the Coriolis Force
CL13 Horizontal Motion - Geostrophic Balance and Friction
tryit: Move the latitude from 45° N to the equator: f → 0 and the inertial radius diverges (no rotation felt). Go to the Southern Hemisphere: the circles reverse and the geostrophic wind flips. Slide friction up: the wind crosses the isobars.

title: Ice–albedo feedback: multiple climates from one Sun
desc: Zero-dimensional energy balance: absorbed sunlight S(1 − α(T))/4 against emitted radiation εσT⁴, with the planetary albedo α rising when the surface freezes. Where the curves cross the climate is in equilibrium: stable (the slope of absorbed − emitted is negative) or unstable. For some solar constants there are three equilibria (warm, unstable, snowball Earth) and the climate shows hysteresis when S is slowly changed.
chapters: CL04 Feedback and Multiple Steady States
CL03 Radiation and Planetary Energy Balance
tryit: Set S/S₀ = 1: warm climate near 290 K and a cold, ice-covered state near 247 K, separated by an unstable state. Reduce S/S₀ until the warm state vanishes (jump to snowball); raise it back: the return jump happens at a much higher S/S₀.

title: The layer greenhouse model
desc: Absorbed sunlight S(1 − α)/4 is balanced by outgoing longwave radiation. Put N atmospheric layers above the surface, each absorbing a fraction ε of the infrared passing through and re-emitting up and down. For black layers (ε = 1) the surface is (N+1)^{1/4} times the emission temperature (255 K): more layers or more absorption, a warmer surface and a colder top of the atmosphere.
chapters: CL08 Greenhouse Models
CL09 Radiative-Convective Equilibrium
tryit: N = 1, ε = 1: surface 303 K (= 255·2^{1/4}). N = 0 gives 255 K, no greenhouse effect. Reduce ε to see the real, partly transparent atmosphere (for one layer σT_s⁴(1 − ε/2) = S(1−α)/4, so T_s = 288 K needs ε = 0.78).

title: Blackbody spectra: why sunlight is shortwave and Earth glows in the infrared
desc: Planck's law B_λ(T) on a log wavelength axis for any temperature, with the visible band shaded. The Sun (≈5772 K) peaks in the visible near 0.5 µm; the Earth (≈288 K) peaks near 10 µm. Wien's displacement law λ_max T = 2898 µm K and the Stefan–Boltzmann law F = σT⁴ are read off live. The overlap of the two curves is tiny, which is what lets us treat shortwave and longwave separately.
chapters: CL03 Radiation and Planetary Energy Balance
CL07 Optical Properties of the Atmosphere
tryit: Drag T from 288 K to 5772 K and watch the peak slide through the visible; compare the areas (T⁴).

title: Brachistochrone: which path is fastest?
desc: A bead slides from rest from the origin to the end point under gravity along four paths. Drag the end point or change the exponent of the trial path; the cycloid always wins. Press race to watch the beads.
chapters: CM01 Variational Calculus and Hamilton's Principle
tryit: Drag the exponent p of the power-law path (p = 1 is the straight line) and watch its time exceed the cycloid's; then increase the depth Y beyond X to make the cycloid dip below the end point.

title: Is the action a minimum? The second variation
desc: Oscillator with ω = 2 between fixed endpoints x(0)=0, x(T)=1. The true path makes the action stationary; adding a wiggle ε·sin(nπt/T) changes S by (mT/4)ε²[(nπ/T)² − ω²]. Slide the duration T past π/ω and watch the parabola flip from a minimum to a saddle.
chapters: CM01 Variational Calculus and Hamilton's Principle
tryit: Move T through π/ω = 1.571: for n = 1 the curvature of S(ε) changes sign exactly there. Raise n and see that higher modes stay stabilising until ωT > nπ.

title: Leaving the hemisphere: the Lagrange multiplier is the normal force
desc: A mass slides without friction from near the top of a hemisphere. While it stays on the surface, the multiplier gives the normal force N = Mg(3cos θ − 2); it leaves where N = 0, at cos θ = 2/3 (θ = 48.19°) with v² = (2/3)ga, and flies off as a projectile.
chapters: CM02 Lagrange's Equations, Constraints and Generalised Coordinates
tryit: Change the tiny initial push: the leaving angle does not depend on it (for a start from rest at the top). Watch N/Mg fall to zero as the bead reaches 48.19° and see the parabola take over.

title: Bead on a rotating hoop: a pitchfork bifurcation
desc: A smooth bead on a hoop of radius R that spins about its vertical diameter at Ω. The effective potential U(θ) = −gR cos θ − ½R²Ω² sin²θ has one minimum at the bottom for Ω below √(g/R) and two off-centre minima above it. Drop the bead and watch it settle (with a little friction) or oscillate.
chapters: CM02 Lagrange's Equations, Constraints and Generalised Coordinates
CM03 Symmetries, Noether's Theorem and Conservation Laws
tryit: Sweep Ω through √(g/R) = 4.43 rad/s and watch the bottom of the hoop become a maximum while two new minima appear at cos θ₀ = g/(Ω²R).

title: Noether in action: which symmetry conserves what?
desc: A particle moves in the plane in one of three potentials. Watch the four candidate conserved quantities p_x, p_y, L_z = x p_y − y p_x and E over time: only those that match a symmetry of the potential stay flat. Isotropic well → L_z and E; well depending on x only (translation symmetry in y) → p_y and E; anisotropic well → only E.
chapters: CM03 Symmetries, Noether's Theorem and Conservation Laws
tryit: Cycle through the three potentials with the same initial condition and see which curves become flat lines.

title: Orbits in a central force: precession and the effective potential
desc: A particle of unit mass moves in F = −r^n toward the centre. The orbit (left) and the effective potential U_eff = M²/2r² + U(r) with the energy line (right) are shown together. n = −2 is Kepler; n = 1 is the harmonic oscillator. Any other n gives a precessing rosette with apsidal angle π/β, β² = 3 + n.
chapters: CM04 Central Forces and Effective One-Dimensional Motion
tryit: Set n = −2: closed ellipse. Change to −2.1: the perihelion advances 19.5° per orbit. Try n = −3 (marginal), and speeds above √2 × circular for escape when n = −2.

title: Scattering: from impact parameter to cross-section
desc: A uniform beam of unit-mass particles with equally spaced impact parameters hits a fixed repulsive Coulomb centre (or a hard sphere). Each trajectory is integrated; the lower panel shows the deflection angle χ(p) and the histogram of how many particles land in each angle against Rutherford's dσ/dΩ ∝ 1/sin⁴(χ/2).
chapters: CM05 Scattering
tryit: Increase the strength α/mv²: the deflections grow and the curve p = (α/mv²)cot(χ/2) steepens. Switch to hard sphere and see the isotropic (flat) dσ/dΩ = a²/4.

title: Two coupled oscillators: normal modes and beats
desc: Two equal masses on springs with a coupling spring. Choose how much of the in-phase mode (frequency ω₁ = √(ω₀² − α)) and the anti-phase mode (ω₂ = √(ω₀² + α)) you start with. Pure modes oscillate rigidly; a mixture beats, passing energy back and forth with period 2π/(ω₂ − ω₁).
chapters: CM06 Small Oscillations and Normal Modes
tryit: Start with all of the motion in the in-phase mode, then all in the anti-phase mode, then 50/50 (x=1, y=0): that is the full-transfer beat. Increase the coupling α to speed the beats.

title: Double pendulum: linear normal modes versus the real thing
desc: Equal masses and rods. For small angles the motion is a superposition of two normal modes with ω² = (2 ∓ √2) g/l and mode shapes (1, ±√2). Pick a mode and a starting amplitude: at small amplitude the real nonlinear pendulum follows the linear prediction; at large amplitude, or from a generic start, it becomes chaotic: two nearly identical starts (blue and orange) soon disagree completely.
chapters: CM06 Small Oscillations and Normal Modes
tryit: Choose 'slow mode' at amplitude 0.05 rad: clean periodic motion with period 2.621 s. Raise the amplitude to 1.5 rad or choose 'generic' and watch the two copies diverge.

title: Driven damped oscillator: resonance curve, phase and transient
desc: x'' + b x' + ω₀²x = cos(γt), ω₀ = 2. Left: the steady-state amplitude and phase lag as a function of the driving frequency γ, with the current γ marked. Right: the actual motion from rest, which is the steady state plus a decaying transient (beats when damping is small, linear growth at resonance with b = 0).
chapters: CM06 Small Oscillations and Normal Modes
tryit: Set b = 0 and γ = ω₀: the amplitude grows ∝ t sin ω₀t. Put γ = 2.1 for beats with period 62.8. Then add damping and see the peak height ~ 1/(bω₀).

title: Displacement current: charging a capacitor
desc: A circular parallel-plate capacitor (plate radius R) is charged by a steady current I. Ampère's law needs both the conduction current through a loop and the displacement current ε₀ dΦ_E/dt: with the flat disc surface the whole answer comes from the displacement term, with the balloon surface through the wire from the conduction current. Move the Amperian loop and compare B(r) with and without the displacement term.
chapters: ED03 Maxwell's Equations and Boundary Conditions
tryit: Drag r across the plate radius R: B grows linearly inside the gap (only the part of the displacement current enclosed counts) and falls as 1/r outside, joining the wire's field. Untick 'include displacement current' to see Ampère's law fail (B = 0 in the gap).

title: Where does the energy flow? The Poynting vector
desc: S = E × B/μ₀ shows the path of electromagnetic energy. In a current-carrying resistive wire the energy enters through the side, radially inward; in a charging capacitor it enters through the rim of the gap; in a plane wave it travels along k. Pick a scenario and adjust the numbers: the integral of S through the surface always equals the power delivered (VI, or dU/dt).
chapters: ED04 Conservation Laws - Energy, Momentum, Angular Momentum
tryit: Wire: raise the current I and watch the inward flux keep equalling I²R. Capacitor: let the plates charge and compare the Poynting flux through the rim with dU/dt. Wave: check that S = c u for any polarisation.

title: Polarization of light: from linear through elliptical to circular
desc: E = (a₁ cos(ωt), a₂ cos(ωt + δ)) for a wave travelling along z. The tip of E traces a straight line, an ellipse or a circle. Change the two amplitudes and the phase lag δ; the Stokes parameters, the sense of rotation (helicity) and the ellipse axes are shown live. Right: the instantaneous wave along z as a spiral.
chapters: ED05 Electromagnetic Waves in Vacuum
tryit: δ = 0: linear. δ = 90° with a₁ = a₂: circular. Keep δ = 90° and shrink a₂: elliptical with axes along x and y. Choose δ = 60°, a₁ = 3, a₂ = 4 for the Stokes numbers in ED05.

title: Reflection and refraction: Snell, Fresnel, Brewster, total internal reflection
desc: A plane wave meets a flat interface between media of index n₁ and n₂. Set the angle of incidence: the rays show the reflected and transmitted directions (Snell), the curves show the reflected fraction for E parallel and perpendicular to the plane of incidence (Fresnel), with the Brewster and critical angles marked. Beyond the critical angle the transmitted wave becomes an evanescent field with the decay length shown.
chapters: ED06 Waves in Matter, Reflection and Dispersion
tryit: n₁ = 1, n₂ = 1.5: the parallel curve touches zero at the Brewster angle 56.3°. Swap to n₁ = 1.5, n₂ = 1: total internal reflection beyond 41.8°, with an evanescent decay length ~λ/(2π√(sin²θ − sin²θ_c)).

title: Dispersion and absorption: the Lorentz oscillator and the plasma
desc: Electrons modelled as damped springs give ε(ω) = 1 + ω_P²/(ω₀² − ω² − iγω). Top: refractive index n(ω) and absorption α(ω) near one resonance. Below the resonance n rises with frequency (normal dispersion, blue bends more than red); inside the absorption line n falls (anomalous dispersion). Bottom: a free-electron plasma ω² = ω_p² + c²k², with phase velocity above c and group velocity below c.
chapters: ED06 Waves in Matter, Reflection and Dispersion
tryit: Narrow the damping γ and watch the anomalous region shrink onto the absorption peak. Move the probe frequency in the plasma panel below ω_p: k becomes imaginary and the wave cannot propagate.

title: Rectangular waveguide: cutoff, modes and the bouncing wave
desc: A hollow metal pipe of cross-section a × b. Each TE_mn mode has a cutoff frequency f_mn = (c/2)√((m/a)² + (n/b)²); below it the wave is evanescent. Choose the guide size, the mode and the frequency: left, the transverse electric field pattern; right, the cutoff ladder with your operating frequency, and the zig-zag path of the equivalent bouncing plane wave with phase velocity above c and group velocity below c.
chapters: ED07 Guided Waves
tryit: With a = 2.28 cm, b = 1.01 cm sweep the frequency from 5 to 18 GHz and count the modes that switch on (TE10 at 6.57, TE20 at 13.15, TE01 at 14.84, TE11 at 16.23 GHz). At 10 GHz the bounce angle is 41.1°.

title: Gauge freedom: change A, keep the fields
desc: A gauge transformation A → A + ∇λ, V → V − ∂λ/∂t changes the potentials but not E or B. Left: a uniform magnetic field B ẑ drawn with the Landau potential A = (0, Bx) plus ∇λ for λ = c₁xy + c₂(x² − y²)/2: the arrow field of A changes wildly while the curl (colour) stays exactly B. Right: a uniform electric field E₀ represented either by V = −E₀x with A = 0, or by V = 0 with A = −E₀t x̂, and everything in between.
chapters: ED08 Potentials and Gauge Transformations
tryit: Move c₁: the arrows rotate toward the symmetric gauge (c₁ = −B/2 gives A = (B/2)(−y, x)) yet the colour map of B does not change. On the right drag the mixing slider from the static V picture to the time-dependent A picture: E = −∇V − ∂A/∂t is identical.

title: Two competitors: isoclines decide who wins
desc: Lotka–Volterra competition: dN₁/dt = r₁N₁(K₁ − N₁ − α₁₂N₂)/K₁ and the mirror equation for species 2. The zero-growth isoclines are straight lines; which one lies outside the other fixes the outcome: species 1 wins, species 2 wins, stable coexistence (each limits itself more than the other, α₁₂α₂₁ < 1 with the K conditions) or an unstable equilibrium (priority effect). Click anywhere in the plane to start a trajectory.
chapters: EE04 Competition and Invasions
tryit: K₁ = 100, K₂ = 80, α₁₂ = 0.5, α₂₁ = 0.6 → stable coexistence at (85.7, 28.6). Set both α = 1.5 → saddle at (16, 56): click on either side of the separatrix and watch the winner change.

title: Shallow lakes: alternative stable states and hysteresis
desc: A single variable x (phosphorus / turbidity) obeys dx/dt = a − b x + r f(x), f(x) = xᵖ/(xᵖ + hᵖ): loading a, removal b, a sigmoidal internal recycling term. When the recycling is steep enough (max r f′ > b) the equilibrium curve folds over: for a between the two fold points a lake can be clear or turbid. Slowly raise and then lower the loading to see the lake jump at one fold and return only at the other (hysteresis). Left: the balance diagram; right: the equilibrium curve with the lake's state.
chapters: EE06 Eutrophication and Alternative Stable States
tryit: b = 1, r = 1.4, h = 1, p = 8: bistable for 0.050 < a < 0.626. Press 'sweep loading up and down' and see the jump up at a = 0.626 and the jump down only at a = 0.050. Reduce r (or p) until the S-curve disappears: no hysteresis.

title: Age-structured growth: the Leslie matrix settles into a stable age distribution
desc: Four age classes with fecundities F and survivals P: n_{t+1} = L n_t. Start from any age mix and watch the oscillations die away: the total grows like λᵗ and the proportions in each class converge to the same stable age distribution, the dominant eigenvector. The Euler–Lotka equation Σ F_x l_x λ^{−x} = 1 gives λ, and λ > 1 exactly when the net reproductive rate R₀ > 1.
chapters: EE02 Structured Population Models
tryit: Defaults P = (0.5, 0.2, 0.1), F = (0, 2, 1, 1) and 200 newborns reproduce the slide: λ = 1.05082, SAD (0.635, 0.302, 0.057, 0.005). Lower F₂ until R₀ < 1 and the population dies out. Start with all adults instead of newborns to change the transient, not the limit.

title: Predator–prey cycles: closed orbits and damped spirals
desc: Lotka–Volterra: dH/dt = rH(1 − H/K) − pHP, dP/dt = apHP − mP. With K = ∞ (prey growth exponential) every orbit is a closed curve around (H*, P*) = (m/ap, r/p); a conserved quantity V labels them. Turn on a finite carrying capacity K and the centre becomes a stable spiral: the cycles damp. Left: phase plane with isoclines and the vector field; right: time series, with the predator peak lagging the prey peak.
chapters: EE05 Predation
tryit: Defaults r=1, p=0.02, a=0.5, m=0.5 give (H*,P*) = (50,50) and period 8.9 for small cycles; the large orbit from (30,30) has period 9.26. Set K = 200: the equilibrium moves to (50, 37.5), eigenvalues −0.125 ± 0.60i. Double r: predators double, prey unchanged.

title: From a stable point to chaos: the Ricker map
desc: n_{t+1} = n_t exp[r(1 − n_t/K)] with K = 100. The time series, the cobweb diagram (vertical to the curve, horizontal to the 45° line) and the bifurcation diagram are linked to one slider r. The fixed point K loses stability at r = 2 (slope 1 − r reaches −1), then 2-, 4-, 8-cycles, chaos from r ≈ 2.69, with periodic windows. Switch on the second run started 10⁻⁶ away to see sensitive dependence on initial conditions, and read off the Lyapunov exponent.
chapters: EE03 Population Dynamics and Chaos
tryit: r = 1.3 (damped), 2.3 (2-cycle 159.2/40.8), 2.6 (4-cycle), 3.0 (chaos, Λ = +0.39), 3.6 (periodic window, Λ < 0). With the second run on at r = 3.0 the two series part after ~35 steps.

title: The dihedral group D_n: symmetries, the Cayley table and cosets
desc: Act on a labelled regular n-gon with the rotation r (by 2π/n) and the reflection s. Every state is r^a s^b, the group has 2n elements, and rs ≠ sr (the group is non-abelian for n ≥ 3, with srs = r⁻¹). The Cayley table is coloured by element, so every row and column is a permutation of the colours (cancellation). Pick any element g: the cyclic subgroup ⟨g⟩ is found and the left cosets aH are shown (they partition the group into equal blocks, Lagrange).
chapters: GT01 Groups Subgroups and Cosets
GT06 Permutation Groups
tryit: n = 3 gives D₃ ≅ S₃: press r, then s, and compare with s then r (a different state). Choose g = s: the cosets are {1,s}, {r, rs}, {r², r²s} (3 cosets of size 2). Choose g = r in D₄: ⟨r⟩ has order 4, index 2: a normal subgroup.

title: Permutations: cycles, order and sign
desc: A permutation of {1..n} drawn as arrows i → σ(i) on a circle. Its disjoint cycle decomposition, cycle type (the conjugacy class in S_n), order (lcm of the cycle lengths) and sign (−1)^{n − #cycles} are read off live. Multiply by a transposition (swap two entries) and the sign flips; the number of even permutations is exactly half of n!. Random permutations show the typical cycle structure.
chapters: GT06 Permutation Groups
GT04 Commutators Simple Groups and Composition Series
tryit: Build a 3-cycle (1 2 3): order 3, sign +. Multiply by a transposition: sign flips. The preset (1 2)(3 4 5) has order lcm(2,3) = 6 and sign −1 (odd). Swap two values and watch the cycle structure merge or split and the sign flip. Press 'random' repeatedly to see typical cycle types.

title: Elastic plates: flexure under a load, and the plate as a low-pass filter
desc: A lithospheric plate of elastic thickness T_e and flexural rigidity D = E T_e³/12(1−ν²) floating on the mantle bends under a line load: w(x) = w₀ e^(−x/α)[cos(x/α) + sin(x/α)] with flexural parameter α = (4D/Δρg)^(1/4), a depression with a small forebulge. Right: how much of a surface load of wavelength λ is compensated by the plate: 1/(1+(k/k_c)⁴), half at λ = 2π(D/Δρg)^(1/4). Thin plates follow topography locally (Airy), thick plates carry short loads.
chapters: LS10 Folds Flexure and Mountain Building
LS07 Isostasy
tryit: T_e = 25 km, Δρ = 3300: D ≈ 9.7×10²² N m and half-compensation at λ ≈ 262 km (D = 10²³ N m gives 263 km). Increase T_e (10, 30, 50, 70 km): the depression widens and shallows and the forebulge moves outward. Fill the basin with sediment (Δρ smaller) and α grows.

title: Ice sheets and valley glaciers: profiles from flow and mass balance
desc: Left: the steady ice-sheet profile from Glen's law (Vialov): H^((2n+2)/n) = H₀^((2n+2)/n)[1 − (x/L)^((n+1)/n)], compared with the perfectly plastic parabola H = √(2Cx/ρ_i g) (the n → ∞ limit); the thickness scales as √L either way. Right: a valley glacier with mass-balance profile b(x) = γ(x_E − x): the ice flux Q(x) = Wγ(x_E x − x²/2) is maximal at the equilibrium line and returns to zero at the terminus x = 2x_E.
chapters: LS14 Glaciers Mass Balance and Ice Flow
tryit: Plastic panel: x = 400 km gives H = √(22.2 m × 400 km) = 3.0 km (Greenland). Raise n: the Vialov curve approaches the plastic one. Right: γ = 2 m/yr per km, x_E = 3 km, W = 1 km → Q_max = 9×10⁶ m³/yr, terminus 6 km, 90 m/yr at the ELA if H = 100 m.

title: Hillslope diffusion: scarp degradation and the steady convex hillslope
desc: Soil creep makes the downslope sediment flux proportional to slope, q = −κ ∂z/∂x, so topography obeys ∂z/∂t = U + κ ∂²z/∂x². Left: an initially vertical scarp of height h smooths into z = −(h/2) erf(x/2√(κt)); its steepest slope falls as t^(−1/2), which lets you date it from κt = h²/(4π S_max²). Right: a ridge under steady uplift grows from flat into the parabola z = (U/2κ)(L² − x²), relief UL²/2κ, on a time scale L²/κ (finite-difference simulation).
chapters: LS12 Hillslope Transport and the Diffusion Equation
tryit: Left: h = 4 m, κ = 0.005 m²/yr, t = 6400 yr gives S_max = 0.2 and κt = 32 m². Right: κ = 0.005 m²/yr, U = 30 m/Myr, L = 100 m: relief 30 m, base slope 0.6, response time 2 Myr.

title: Airy isostasy: why mountains have roots, and glacial rebound
desc: Columns of crust float on the denser mantle like blocks of wood in water. Equal mass above a compensation depth fixes the root under a mountain, b₁ = ρ_c h₁/(ρ_m − ρ_c), and the thinning under an ocean basin, b₂ = (ρ_c − ρ_w)h₂/(ρ_m − ρ_c). Change the densities and heights and the three columns re-float. Right: after a load (ice) is removed the crust rebounds exponentially with relaxation time τ = 4πμ/(ρ g λ).
chapters: LS07 Isostasy
LS15 Glacial Deposits Rebound and Sea Level
tryit: With ρ_c = 2800, ρ_m = 3300 the root is 5.6 × the height: a 5 km plateau has a 28 km root and a 68 km crust. Raise ρ_c toward ρ_m and the roots get enormous; lower it and they shrink. In the rebound panel, make the mantle less viscous and watch τ shrink.

title: Waves coming ashore: dispersion, shoaling, refraction and breaking
desc: Linear water waves obey ω² = g k tanh(kh): in deep water the phase speed is gT/2π, in shallow water √(gh). A swell of period T and deep-water height H₀ arriving at angle α₀ over a sloping bed shortens, slows, turns toward the beach (Snell), and grows (energy flux conservation: H = H₀ K_s K_r) until it breaks when H reaches about 0.78h. Animated cross-section with the wavelength and height computed from the exact dispersion relation at each depth.
chapters: LS26 Sea Level and Ocean Waves
LS27 Coasts Beaches Deltas and Rocky Shores
tryit: T = 12 s, H₀ = 2 m, α₀ = 30°: at 100 m depth C = 18.6 m/s, K_s = 0.984; at 10 m C = 9.4, K_s = 1.044, K_r = 0.946, α = 14.6°. T = 8 s, H₀ = 1 m, normal incidence breaks at 1.64 m depth with H_b = 1.28 m. Steeper beach: the same waves, nearer the shore.

title: Bedrock rivers: steady profile, slope–area scaling and the knickpoint wave
desc: Stream-power incision E = K Aᵐ Sⁿ balanced against rock uplift U gives the steady slope S = (U/K)^(1/n) A^(−m/n) = k_s A^(−θ), concavity θ = m/n. With Hack's law A ∝ x^1.67 this is a concave-up profile. Press 'step uplift': the river is out of balance, a knickpoint (steepened reach) travels upstream at speed K Aᵐ (n = 1) and the whole profile steepens to the new steady state. Right: the slope–area plot (log–log), parallel lines for different U.
chapters: LS23 Bedrock Channels and River Incision
LS22 Floods Planform and River Profiles
LS16 Fluvial Landscapes
tryit: m = 0.5, n = 1, K = 5×10⁻⁶ yr⁻¹ and U = 0.5 mm/yr give S = 100 A^(−1/2): S = 0.1 at 1 km² and 0.01 at 100 km². Step U by ×4: at n = 1 every slope quadruples (steady state), at n = 19/16 only 4^(16/19) = 3.2. Watch the knickpoint reach the divide.

title: Moving sediment: Shields threshold and the Rouse suspension profile
desc: A flow moves a grain when the bed shear stress τ_b = ρ g H S exceeds the threshold τ_c = θ_c (ρ_s − ρ) g D (Shields). The largest movable grain is D = τ_b/[θ_c(ρ_s − ρ)g]. Once moving, a grain is held up by turbulence if its settling velocity w_s is small compared with κu_*; the Rouse number P = w_s/(κ u_*) sets the concentration profile C(z)/C_a = [((H−z)/z)(a/(H−a))]^P, from nearly uniform silt to a bedload sand layer.
chapters: LS24 Sediment Transport Mechanics
tryit: S = 0.003, H = 1.2 m: τ_b = 35 Pa and the largest mobile grain is 48 mm gravel (Shields number 0.045). Then set H = 3 m, S = 10⁻³ (u_* = 0.172 m/s) and move D from 0.05 to 5 mm: P goes 0.03 → 4.7, and C(0.5H)/C_a drops from 0.91 to 10⁻⁶.

title: The Hodgkin–Huxley neuron: threshold, all-or-none spikes and repetitive firing
desc: The squid-axon membrane model: C dV/dt = I − g_Na m³h (V − E_Na) − g_K n⁴ (V − E_K) − g_L (V − E_L), with three gating variables m, h, n relaxing toward voltage-dependent targets. Kick the membrane by a few millivolts: below threshold the voltage just decays, above it a full spike (≈ +40 mV) fires regardless of how hard you kicked (all-or-none). Inject constant current to get repetitive firing, or block the sodium or potassium channels.
chapters: Neuroscience - Course Map
tryit: Rest is −65 mV. A kick of 6 mV decays, 7 mV fires a spike peaking near +37 mV; 15 mV peaks at +40 mV, hardly higher. Constant current: no spikes below about 6 µA/cm², then a steady train (≈ 60 Hz at 7, 87 Hz at 20). Block Na⁺ (TTX) and no spike is possible; block K⁺ (TEA) and the spike will not repolarise properly.

title: The ε–δ game: continuity and limits made visible
desc: For a function f and a point a, an adversary picks a tolerance ε around f(a) (horizontal band); you must answer with a δ so that every x within δ of a lands inside the band. Choose the function: smooth ones always have an answer (shown as the largest δ that works), the jump discontinuity has none once ε is below the jump, sin(1/x) near 0 has none for any small ε, and 1/x shows how δ depends on the point a (continuous but not uniformly continuous).
chapters: PA06 The Real Numbers and Sequences
PA13 The Derivative and the Inverse Function Theorem
tryit: f(x) = x² at a = 1, ε = 0.1: δ = √1.1 − 1 or 1 − √0.9, the smaller is 0.0488. Move a toward 3: δ shrinks (the same ε needs smaller δ where the graph is steeper). Choose the step function: ε = 0.3 fails for every δ.

title: Metric balls: the same plane, different geometries
desc: The ball B(p, r) = {x : d(x,p) < r} for the ℓᵖ metric d_p(x,y) = (|x₁−y₁|ᵖ + |x₂−y₂|ᵖ)^{1/p}: a diamond for p = 1 (taxicab), a disc for p = 2, a square for p = ∞. Move the centre, radius and p; click a point to test membership. Also: the discrete metric (every ball of radius ≤ 1 is a single point), the 'river' (British Rail / SNCF) metric, and a check that every point of an open ball has a smaller ball inside it (open sets).
chapters: PA07 Metric and Topological Spaces
PA11 Subspaces, Products and Quotients
tryit: p = 1, 2, ∞ with r = 1: area 2, π, 4. Slide p between 1 and ∞ and the diamond bulges into a square. In the discrete metric the ball B(p, 1) is {p} and B(p, 1.01) is everything. Click a point and watch the triangle inequality hold.

title: Picard iteration: building the solution of an ODE step by step
desc: For y′ = f(t, y), y(0) = y₀, the Picard iterates yₖ₊₁(t) = y₀ + ∫₀ᵗ f(s, yₖ(s)) ds converge to the solution when f is Lipschitz in y (contraction mapping). Choose an ODE and step through the iterates: y′ = y gives the partial sums of eᵗ; y′ = y² gives partial sums of the geometric series 1/(1−t) and the true solution blows up at t = 1 (existence only locally); y′ = 3y^{2/3} from y(0) = 0 is not Lipschitz and has more than one solution.
chapters: PA14 ODE Existence Uniqueness and Smooth Dependence
tryit: y′ = y: the k-th iterate is 1 + t + … + tᵏ/k!. y′ = y²: iterates 1, 1 + t, 1 + t + t² + …; they only converge for |t| < 1, even though f is smooth (a finite escape time). y′ = 3y^{2/3}, y(0) = 0: both y = 0 and y = t³ solve it.

title: Bayes' rule as a picture: why a positive test is often a false alarm
desc: 10 000 people, drawn as dots in four blocks: ill and positive (true positives), ill and negative, healthy and positive (false positives), healthy and negative. The posterior P(ill | +) is the red block's share of all positive dots. Move the prevalence, the sensitivity and the false-positive rate: when the disease is rare the false-positive block swamps the true positives even for an accurate test. A second panel plots the posterior against the prevalence, and a button repeats the test.
chapters: PR02 Conditional Probability Bayes Rule and Independence
tryit: Defaults 0.5 %, 95 %, 1 %: 47.5 true positives vs 99.5 false positives, posterior 0.323. Set prevalence 1 %, sensitivity 95 %, false-positive 5 %: posterior 0.161. Press 'second positive test' and the posterior becomes the new prior.

title: Binomial → Poisson and binomial → normal
desc: Bars: the exact Binomial(n, p) probabilities. Dots: the Poisson(np) approximation (good when n is large and p small). Curve: the normal N(np, np(1−p)) approximation (good when np(1−p) is large). The total-variation distances to each approximation are computed live, so you can see where each limit works and where it fails.
chapters: PR03 Discrete Random Variables and Distributions
PR06 Moments Generating Functions and Limit Theorems
tryit: n = 100, p = 0.02: Poisson(2) is superb, the normal is poor (skewed, negative values). n = 100, p = 0.5: normal superb, Poisson terrible. Fix np = 5 and increase n: binomial → Poisson(5).

title: The central limit theorem in action
desc: Draw n independent values from a distribution (uniform, exponential, a very skewed Bernoulli, a two-point distribution or a heavy-tailed log-normal), average them, standardise, and repeat 4000 times. The histogram of the standardised mean approaches the standard normal curve as n grows, whatever the starting shape, with skewness shrinking like γ/√n. The single-draw distribution is shown on the left for comparison.
chapters: PR06 Moments Generating Functions and Limit Theorems
tryit: Exponential (skewness 2): n = 1 is a one-sided exponential curve; n = 4 is already lump-shaped; n = 30 is close to normal, skewness 2/√n = 0.37. The log-normal needs a much larger n. Bernoulli(0.05) needs n around 100 before the normal shape appears (the usual rule np ≥ 10).

title: Covariance, correlation and what they miss
desc: A cloud of 300 points with a chosen shape. For a bivariate normal the correlation ρ controls the tilt and the regression line; ρ = 0 means independent. But zero correlation does not imply independence: y = x² and a circle are completely dependent yet uncorrelated (symmetry kills the linear term). An outlier slider shows how fragile the sample correlation is. The regression line y = ρ(σ_y/σ_x)x and R² = ρ² are drawn.
chapters: PR07 Sums of Independent Variables Covariance and Correlation
tryit: Bivariate normal, ρ = 0.8: R² = 0.64. Switch to the parabola: correlation ≈ 0 despite y being a function of x. Add an outlier at (6, 6) to uncorrelated normal data and the correlation jumps.

title: Particle in a box: build a state from energy eigenstates
desc: Infinite well of width 1 (ħ = m = 1), E_n = n²π²/2. Choose the amplitudes of the first four eigenstates: a single eigenstate has a frozen |ψ|²; a superposition has |ψ|² that sloshes back and forth at the Bohr frequencies E_m − E_n, and the energy expectation value stays constant. The probability of each energy is |c_n|².
chapters: QM04 The Particle in a Box
QM03 States Operators and Measurement
tryit: Put equal weight on n = 1 and 2: the packet bounces with period 2π/(E₂−E₁) = 0.85. Add n = 3 and the motion is no longer a simple oscillation. Notice ⟨E⟩ never moves.

title: Finite square well: graphical solution of the bound states
desc: For a well of depth V₀ and width 2a, define z₀ = a√(2mV₀)/ħ. Bound states sit where √(z₀² − ξ²) crosses ξ tan ξ (even states) or −ξ cot ξ (odd states). Slide z₀: new bound states appear each time z₀ passes a multiple of π/2, and there is always at least one (even) state. The wavefunctions are drawn at their energies, leaking into the forbidden region.
chapters: QM07 The Finite Square Well
tryit: Shrink z₀ below π/2: only the ground state remains, even for a very shallow well. Increase z₀ to 10 and compare the lowest energies with the infinite well values (n π/2)².

title: The harmonic oscillator: eigenstates and a coherent state
desc: ħ = m = ω = 1. Left: the eigenstate ψ_n(x) on the parabolic potential, drawn at height E_n with its probability density, with the classical turning points; note the tunnelling into the forbidden region and n nodes. Right: a coherent state |α⟩, a Gaussian that oscillates like a classical particle without changing shape; or an n/n+1 superposition.
chapters: QM05 The Harmonic Oscillator
QM06 The Oscillator Toolbox
tryit: Increase n: the density approaches the classical 1/√(E−V) distribution. Switch to coherent state: ⟨x⟩ follows x_c cos t exactly, and the width stays 1/√2 forever.

title: Spin ½ on the Bloch sphere: Stern–Gerlach and precession
desc: The spin state of a spin-½ particle is a point on the Bloch sphere. A Stern–Gerlach analyser along axis n̂ gives 'up' with probability (1 + n̂·b)/2 and leaves the spin pointing along ±n̂. Run sequential measurements to see the key quantum surprise: z, then x, then z again gives 50 % up at the end. A magnetic field makes the Bloch vector precess at the Larmor frequency.
chapters: QM09 The Stern-Gerlach Experiment and Spin
tryit: Prepare ↑z, measure x (random), then z: the original ↑z is lost, 50 % each. Turn on the field (B along z) and watch the vector precess at constant polar angle.

title: Tunnelling through a barrier: transmission and the standing-wave pattern
desc: A plane wave of energy E hits a rectangular barrier of height V₀ and width 2a (units ħ²/2m = 1). The wavefunction |ψ|² is built from the exact matching solution: standing-wave ripples on the left (interference of incident and reflected waves), exponential decay inside the barrier for E < V₀, and a transmitted wave on the right. T(E) is plotted with your E marked, including the resonances (T = 1) above the barrier.
chapters: QM08 Quantum Tunnelling
QM10 The Finite Barrier and Tutorial V
tryit: Make the barrier wider: T falls like e^{−4κa}. Raise E above V₀: T oscillates and reaches 1 when 2qa = nπ.

title: A free Gaussian wave packet: spreading and the uncertainty principle
desc: A packet ψ(x,0) ∝ exp(−x²/4σ₀² + ik₀x) evolves freely (ħ = m = 1). The real part (oscillating carrier), the probability density |ψ|² and the momentum-space density |φ(k)|² are shown. The centre moves at the group velocity k₀, the width grows as σ(t) = σ₀√(1 + (t/2σ₀²)²), while the momentum spread 1/(2σ₀) never changes: Δx·Δp ≥ ½.
chapters: QM01 From Waves to Probabilities
QM02 The Schrodinger Equation and Stationary States
tryit: Make σ₀ small: it spreads fast (large momentum spread). Make σ₀ large: nearly rigid. Change k₀ and see the packet move without changing shape.

title: The Boltzmann distribution: populations, energy, entropy and heat capacity
desc: A system with energy levels ε_i in contact with a heat bath at temperature T occupies level i with probability p_i = e^{−ε_i/kT}/Z. Pick a level structure (two-level, evenly spaced harmonic ladder, or a rotor-like ε_J = J(J+1)) and sweep the temperature: the populations spread out, U and S rise, and the heat capacity shows its characteristic shape (a Schottky bump for two levels, saturation at k for the oscillator).
chapters: SM03 The Canonical Ensemble
SM07 Equipartition the Virial Theorem and Magnetic Systems
TH06 From Kinetic Theory to Statistical Mechanics
tryit: Two-level: C peaks near kT ≈ 0.42Δ (Schottky anomaly) and falls to zero at both low and high T. Harmonic ladder: C → k only for kT ≫ ħω (equipartition), exponentially frozen below. Watch populations of 'frozen' modes.

title: A gas relaxing to the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution
desc: Hard disks bounce in a box and collide elastically. Start with every particle at the same speed (a very non-equilibrium state): collisions redistribute the energy and the speed histogram relaxes to the 2D Maxwell–Boltzmann form f(v) = (m v/kT) e^{−mv²/2kT}, the picture behind the H-theorem and the approach to equilibrium. The temperature is set by the total kinetic energy.
chapters: SM04 Kinetic Theory and the Boltzmann Equation
TH06 From Kinetic Theory to Statistical Mechanics
SM06 Entropy Information and the Arrow of Time
tryit: Press 'all same speed' and watch the histogram (blue) broaden into the dashed Maxwell–Boltzmann curve within a few collisions per particle. Press 'one fast particle' to see the energy spread out. Turn collisions off and the distribution never changes.

title: The 2D Ising model: a phase transition you can see
desc: A square lattice of spins s = ±1 with nearest-neighbour coupling J (set to 1) and an external field h, simulated with the Metropolis algorithm. At low temperature the lattice orders (magnetisation ±1); at high temperature it is disordered; at the critical temperature T_c = 2/ln(1 + √2) ≈ 2.269 there are fluctuations on all length scales. Onsager's exact T_c and spontaneous magnetisation are shown for comparison.
chapters: SM07 Equipartition the Virial Theorem and Magnetic Systems
SM03 The Canonical Ensemble
tryit: Quench from T = 5 to T = 1: domains coarsen. Sit at T ≈ 2.27 and watch clusters of every size. Apply a field h ≠ 0 below T_c to see the first-order flip of the magnetisation at h = 0.

title: Why equilibrium is overwhelmingly likely: multiplicity and entropy
desc: Two Einstein solids exchange q_tot quanta of energy. The number of microstates for a given split is Ω_A(q_A)·Ω_B(q_tot − q_A); the total is sharply peaked at the split that maximises S = k ln Ω. Increase the solid sizes and the peak (relative width ~ 1/√N) becomes a spike. Also: the coin-flip binomial distribution showing the law of large numbers.
chapters: TH09 Microstates Macrostates and Multiplicity
SM01 Probability Large Numbers and Information
SM06 Entropy Information and the Arrow of Time
tryit: With N_A = N_B and q_tot = 100: peak at q_A = 50. Grow N to 300: the relative width shrinks ~1/√N. Make N_A larger than N_B: the energy is shared in proportion to the sizes (equal temperatures).

title: Fermions, bosons and classical particles: occupation numbers
desc: Mean occupation of a single-particle level of energy ε: Fermi–Dirac n = 1/(e^{(ε−μ)/kT}+1), Bose–Einstein n = 1/(e^{(ε−μ)/kT}−1), Maxwell–Boltzmann n = e^{−(ε−μ)/kT}. Fermions never exceed 1 (Pauli), bosons pile up near the chemical potential (and diverge as ε → μ), and all three coincide when n ≪ 1. Lower panel: the Fermi function sharpening into a step as T → 0, and Planck's law from Bose–Einstein statistics with μ = 0.
chapters: SM08 Quantum Ensembles and Identical Particles
SM05 The Grand Canonical Ensemble and Chemical Equilibrium
tryit: Move (ε−μ)/kT through 0: the Bose curve blows up, the Fermi curve passes through ½, the classical curve through 1. For large positive x the three agree. In the Planck panel raise T and watch the peak move as T (Wien) while the area grows as T⁴.

title: Ideal gas processes and the Carnot cycle on a P–V diagram
desc: One mole of ideal gas (choose monatomic γ = 5/3 or diatomic γ = 7/5) goes around a Carnot cycle: isothermal expansion at T_h, adiabatic expansion, isothermal compression at T_c, adiabatic compression. The enclosed area is the net work; the efficiency is 1 − T_c/T_h whatever the gas or the volumes. Watch the state point travel and the heat and work tally.
chapters: TH03 The Ideal Gas and Adiabatic Processes
TH04 The Second Law Carnot Engines and Entropy
tryit: Increase T_h: the cycle widens and η rises. Change the volume ratio: Q_h and W change but η does not. Compare γ = 5/3 and 7/5: different adiabat steepness, same efficiency.

title: Wave packets: phase velocity versus group velocity
desc: A packet is a superposition of plane waves ψ(x,t) = ∫ A(k) e^{i(kx − ω(k)t)} dk with a Gaussian A(k) centred on k₀. Choose the medium (dispersion relation ω(k)): the carrier ripples move at the phase velocity ω/k, the envelope (and the energy) at the group velocity dω/dk, and with dispersion the packet spreads. Markers show both velocities.
chapters: ED06 Waves in Matter, Reflection and Dispersion
ED07 Guided Waves
QM01 From Waves to Probabilities
LS26 Sea Level and Ocean Waves
tryit: Deep water: v_g = v_p/2 (ripples run through the packet). Waveguide/plasma: v_p·v_g = c², ripples faster than c but the packet slower. Schrödinger: ω = k²/2, v_g = 2v_p. Non-dispersive: nothing spreads.

title: Fourier synthesis: build a waveform from harmonics
desc: A periodic function is a sum of sines. Choose a target (square, triangle, sawtooth) and add harmonics one at a time: the partial sum converges, with the Gibbs overshoot of about 9 % at the jumps of the square and sawtooth waves that never goes away. Below, the harmonic amplitudes b_n.
chapters: ED05 Electromagnetic Waves in Vacuum
QM01 From Waves to Probabilities
PR06 Moments Generating Functions and Limit Theorems
tryit: Square wave with N = 1, 3, 9, 49: watch the Gibbs ears sharpen but not shrink (overshoot 8.95 %). Triangle waves converge much faster (1/n² coefficients).

title: Superposition: standing waves and beats
desc: Two sinusoidal waves added together. Equal frequencies travelling in opposite directions give a standing wave with fixed nodes; slightly different frequencies in the same direction give beats whose envelope moves at the group velocity. Change the frequency difference and the relative amplitude and watch the nodes (or the beats) respond.
chapters: CM06 Small Oscillations and Normal Modes
ED05 Electromagnetic Waves in Vacuum
ED07 Guided Waves
tryit: Mode 'opposite directions' with amplitude ratio 1: perfect standing wave with nodes every λ/2. Lower the ratio: nodes fill in (partial standing wave, a travelling part remains). Mode 'beats': the envelope period is 2π/(k₂ − k₁).
